d1.task: Write the feature brief for the trial-class request. Fill User story, Fields to collect, Three acceptance checks, One failure state and Most private detail. In your reasoning explain when your success message appears and why a parent should never see it too early. Hands-on completion: Build a small runnable trial-booking prototype alongside your brief. Use a local mock server or in-memory store. Run one successful save and one forced failure; submit the relevant code, actual output and the fix. Success must appear only after the save response. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
d1.question: Anita's page runs showMessage('Booking saved') on the Book click and only then calls fetch('/api/bookings'). On a weak mobile network the request fails. Which acceptance check should her feature brief state?
options: Show Booking saved when the parent presses Book, since pressing is the action they asked for
Show Booking saved once the page has finished sending the request, even if no reply arrives
Show Booking saved only after the server replies that the row is stored, else a retry message
Show Booking saved after the spinner ends, then quietly retry in the background if needed
d1.explanation: A success message is a promise that the booking exists. Only the server's reply proves the row was stored, so the brief must tie the message to that reply. Showing it on click or after sending tells the parent a lie whenever the network fails.

fields.label: User story
fields.hint: One line: As a parent, I want ..., so that ... Keep it about one action.

fields.label: Fields to collect
fields.hint: List only the fields the tutor truly needs, each with a short reason. Leave out anything nice-to-have.

fields.label: Three acceptance checks
fields.hint: Three testable lines, each a situation and an exact result, for example slot taken, empty name, success.

fields.label: One failure state
fields.hint: What the parent sees when it goes wrong, in plain words, with the next step.

fields.label: Most private detail
options: Parent's phone number
Child's school and class
Preferred slot and time
Parent's full name
fields.hint: Pick the detail you would hide from other parents; explain in your reasoning.

d2.task: Review the AI-written booking handler. Name Two trust failures, rewrite it in Corrected handler, write Three negative tests, and pick Where the price comes from. In your reasoning explain why the browser cannot be trusted for these values. Hands-on completion: Run your corrected handler locally with a spoofed user ID, changed price and repeated request. Submit the handler and actual output for all three cases, then fix a failing case. A paper trace or expected output alone does not count. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
d2.question: A reviewer reads this AI-written line: const { userId, price } = req.body; await db.query('INSERT INTO bookings(user_id, amount) VALUES ($1, $2)', [userId, price]). A parent sends userId 7 and price 0. What is the best review comment?
options: Add a browser check that price is above zero before the form can be sent
The $1 and $2 placeholders already make this safe, so approve it
Validate that userId is a number and price is not negative
Take userId from the session and look up the price from the server's slots table
d2.explanation: Placeholders stop SQL injection but not lying: the browser can send any userId or price. The server must take identity from the session and the price from its own table. Range checks still accept price 1 for a 500 rupee class.

fields.label: Two trust failures
fields.hint: Name both failures in this snippet and what an attacker could do with each, in your own words.

fields.label: Corrected handler
fields.hint: Edit the handler: derive the user from the session, price from the database, and save with a safe query.

fields.label: Three negative tests
fields.hint: Three tests that must fail safely: another user, a tampered price, a duplicate request. Use expect lines.

fields.label: Where the price comes from
options: A slots table on the server, looked up by slot id
A hidden field in the booking form
A value stored in the browser's local storage
The price in the page URL query string
fields.hint: Pick the one source you would trust for the amount charged.

d3.question: Anita's app stores each booking as a batch id and a seat number. Two parents press Book for seat 10 of the Saturday batch in the same second, and the app only checks the list in its own code first. What most reliably stops both from getting the seat?
options: A note saying seats are limited, shown beside the Book button
Tell parents to refresh the page before booking a seat
A database rule allowing each batch and seat pair only once
A two-second wait after the Book button so replies can catch up
d3.explanation: Two requests can both pass a check in code before either one saves. A unique rule in the database is checked at the moment of saving, so the second booking is refused. Notes, refreshing and waiting only reduce the chance, they do not remove it.

fields.label: Tables and columns
fields.hint: SQL CREATE TABLE statements for the records, with primary keys and the foreign key from booking to batch.

fields.label: What must never repeat
options: One row per student per batch
One row per seat number in one batch
One row per phone number overall
One row per booking date and time
fields.hint: Pick the rule you would enforce in the database for last-seat bookings.

fields.label: Private columns and who sees them
fields.hint: Name two private columns and say who may read them: the parent, the tutor, or nobody else.

Submit the handler and actual status/body for each; fix an inconsistent response. Include the artifact or relevant extract, actual test/run results and your improvement in Your reasoning. Plans, invented results and manual walkthroughs alone do not complete this mission.
d4.question: The Pune workshop page sends a student's email to the Register endpoint, and the same email is already on the list. The browser team needs to show a helpful message. Which reply should the contract promise?
options: A 409 reply with an already_registered code
A 200 reply with an empty body, so the page never breaks or shows anything odd
A 500 reply carrying the raw database error text so the team can debug quickly
A 400 reply with no message, because the browser should work out why itself
d4.explanation: The contract should give a clear status and a code the page can turn into a friendly message. An empty 200 hides the problem, raw database text leaks internals, and a bare 400 leaves the browser guessing what went wrong.

fields.label: Method and path
fields.hint: One line such as VERB /api/... naming the action, not the page.

fields.label: Request body
fields.hint: The JSON body as a JavaScript object literal, with every required input and realistic sample values.

fields.label: Success reply
fields.hint: The server line that sends the success status and JSON body when the registration is saved.

fields.label: Status for already registered
options: 409 Conflict
400 Bad Request
422 Unprocessable Entity
200 OK with an error message inside
fields.hint: Pick the status you would return when the same email registers twice.

fields.label: Two error replies
fields.hint: Two different errors, each with status, JSON body and when it happens.

d5.question: The Jaipur form stops quantity above 20 using a browser setting. A cousin sends a direct request for item 7, quantity 5000, while only 12 are in stock. Which check actually stops this order?
options: The maximum value set on the quantity box in the page
A script that disables the Order button after the first click
Hiding the quantity box on small phone screens
The server comparing quantity with stock before saving
d5.explanation: A direct request never touches the page, so the box limit, button script and hiding all get skipped. Only a check on the server, run before saving, sees every request and can refuse this one.

fields.label: Where to check stock
options: In the browser only, for speed
On the server only, at save time
In both, browser for feedback and server as the real guard
Skip it and let the owner fix orders by phone
fields.hint: Pick where the check "quantity is not above stock" must run for the order form.

fields.hint: Improve the weak validator: check name, a 10-digit Indian phone, a known item, and a whole quantity from 1 to stock.

fields.label: Error message for a bad phone
fields.hint: Polite, names the problem and the fix, without blaming the customer.

fields.label: Error message for too many items
fields.hint: Say how many are available and what to do next.

d6.question: You will ask an AI assistant about the bug where parents see Booking confirmed but the tutor's list is empty. Which message to the assistant is both safest and most useful?
options: Repeat steps, expected and actual result, error line, with secrets and phone numbers replaced by placeholders
Paste the whole .env file and a full export of the bookings table, so the assistant can see the entire setup and every parent's details
Only the words: booking broken, please fix it fast
A screenshot of the live admin page showing every parent's name and number
d6.explanation: Steps plus expected and actual results give the assistant something to reason about, and placeholders keep secrets and families' data out. Pasting the .env or customer data leaks private details, and a vague message makes it guess.

fields.hint: Pick the first thing you would do about the missing bookings.

d7.question: Meera is logged in as a parent. She changes the number in the page address from 412 to 413 and sees another family's booking and phone number. Which fix actually closes this gap?
options: Remove the booking number from the page address so it cannot be edited by hand, and hide other families' links
Check on the server that the booking's parent matches the session user, or the user is the tutor
Only return a booking when the visitor is logged in
Use longer random booking numbers and keep the same code
d7.explanation: The server must compare the booking's owner with the person asking, on every request. Hiding the number or lengthening it only makes guessing harder, and a login-only check lets any logged-in family read any booking.

d8.question: A batch has ten seats and the code is canBook(taken, capacity) { return taken <= capacity }. Which single test would catch the mistake in this code?
options: taken is 3 and capacity is 10, a normal booking day, expecting true
taken is 0 and capacity is 10, expecting true
taken is 12 and capacity is 10, expecting false
taken is 10 and capacity is 10, expecting false
d8.explanation: With ten of ten seats taken the batch is full, but less-than-or-equal still says yes. Only the test at the exact limit shows it. Tests far from the limit pass with both the right and the wrong code.

A booking when the batch is full

fields.hint: Pick the test you would automate first and defend it in your reasoning.

d9.question: The preferred-language change was merged and deployed. Within minutes, bookings fail because the new column is required but the form does not send it. What is the safest first recovery move?
options: Revert the merge commit and redeploy, then fix it on a new branch
Edit the live server files by hand until bookings work
Force-push an older copy from your laptop over main
Delete the repository and start again from last month's zip file
d9.explanation: Reverting the merge commit returns the live app to the last working state quickly and keeps the history. Hand edits and force-pushes can lose other work, and deleting everything throws away the record that helps you find the cause.

Rebase then fast-forward for a straight history
Push straight to main to save time

d10.question: Four gaps remain a week before launch: any logged-in family can open another family's booking by changing the number; a typo in the confirmation text; no alert when saving fails; slow loading on mobile data. Which should be fixed first?
options: The typo, because it is a ten-second fix and makes the list of gaps look much shorter
The booking-number gap, since it is easy to try and exposes families' phone numbers
The missing alert, since failures could pass unseen for a whole day and hit several parents
The slow loading, because every family sees it on the first visit and may give up before booking
d10.explanation: Ranking by harm and likelihood puts the booking-number gap first: anyone can try it and it exposes private phone numbers. The alert and the loading time matter, but their harm is smaller, and a quick typo fix does not reduce real risk.
